label: paragraph_title
text: SEX CAUSATION.

label: text
text: Mrs. Monteith Erskine, the wife of Mr. J. M. Erskine, M.P., has published in a book the results of her investigations into sex determination.

label: text
text: In the preface Mrs. Erskine describes how, as a schoolgirl at Geneva, she was led to study works expounding theories on sex-crusation, and she says: "It may be well to answer the constantly repeated question, 'What on earth possessed you, at such an early age, to take up a subject of a nature so peculiar, or, at any rate, controversial?'"

label: text
text: In my own case, Mrs. Erskine proceeds, "a keen sense of the wrong which I had suffered from the start, by being born a girl where a boy was desired, had led mo to vague doubts and questionings in early childhood.... The helplessness of women in respect of any power to determine the sex of their offspring I regarded as a gross injustice and as a palpable reflection on the progress of science..... Then it was that the idea filtered slowly through my brain that it might well be a woman who alone could solve the problem..... Then came marriage, with its attendant responsibilities. Five children were born to me alive and healthy, and they proved to be, as I desired, one girl and four boys."

label: text
text: In July, 1908, acting on the advice of an eminent gymacologist IRS, Erskine states, she deposited with her bankers the actual formula which she had tested for the practical application of her theory, and which she had, in many cases, used to her own complete satisfaction.

label: text
text: "Since 1909," she adds "people from many countries have committed me about their future offering. Letters of acknowledgment and testimony to the efficacy my plans have flowed in from very part of the world."

Is dancing being taken too seriously?

label: text
text: GIRLS WHO LOSE ROSY

label: text
text: Not only in London, but throughout the country, there is an epidemic of "dance-fever," which is daily claiming more and more victims.

label: text
text: In his summing up at an inquest on a married woman who committed suicide while separated from her husband, Mr. Ingleby Oddie, the Westminster coroner, said "The deceased apparently was m'd about dancing. Many people are now d'ys. They treat it not merely as an occasional amusement but as a serious business of life."

label: text
text: A correspondent writes to "The Daily Mail": "I have been to dance halls where I have seen young girls take the floor for as many as 40 dances and leave in a state of partial collapse."

label: text
text: Miss Madge Titheradge, the actress, said to a "Daily Mail" reporter:

label: text
text:
I certainly think that dancing can be overdone. Why should people dance morning, noon, and night? Dancing is a splendid exercise and it can be made quite divine—but like everything else it should be taken in moderation.
There is so much to learn and so much to do that life is far too short to be spent in dance-halls.

label: text
text: If girls gave up cocktails, read fine books, did more sewing and housework, and went to bed earlier they would be all the better for it—and they would keep the roses in their checks.

label: text
text: Lady Askwith said:

label: text
text: If indulged into excess dancing undoubtedly becomes not only harmful but also ridiculous. As a recreation it is an excellent thing, but it loses its virtue when it becomes a craze.

label: text

CHOOSING A CITY MARSHAL
FROM 300.

label: text
text: The task of Paris, son of Priam, who had to decide whether Venus, Minerva, or Juno was the most beautiful, pales into insignificance beside that now facing the City of London Corporation. To the Officers and Clerks Committee falls the delicate business of selecting from some 300 men—all of whom believe themselves to be more than usually good-looking, is this is a vital qualification for the post—a number of suitable candidates for the ancient office of City Marshal, vacant through the retirement through ill-health of Major R. J. Smyly, who was appointed in 1921.

label: text
text: The committee begins its work of elimination and the final choice rests with the Court of Common Council. A section of the council desires to do away with the post on the ground that it is, useless and expensive, and an amendment calling for its abolition is likely to be moved:

label: text
text: The City Marshal, whose office dates from 1570, receives £300 a year, and rides before the Lord Mayor's coach when he goes to the Guildhall onto the Central Criminal Court, so he must be a good horse man.

label: paragraph_title
text: NIGHT CLUB RAIDED

label: text
text: POLICE ATTACK WITH JEMMY.

label: text
text: Evelyn Merrick, Henry Lester Merrick, and Maud Cross appeared at Bow Street charged with selling intoxicants without a licence at the Forty-three or Proctor's Club, Gerrard Street, Soho. Mrs. Merrick was in court. Mr. Muskett, prosecuting, said he withdrew the summonses against Evelyn Merrick, as she was a mere girl. The premises were the despair of the police, for they had been so frequently under notice at that court.

label: text
text: As a result of proceedings against Mrs. Merrick last July the club was struck off the register. In the following October the place was being run by the Merrick family as an unregistered club and Mrs. Merrick and her son Henry were prosecuted. The case against Henry Merrick was then withdrawn and his mother sentenced to six months' imprisonment, from which she had just been released.

label: text
text: During her absence the place had been kept going by her son and two daughters, assisted by Miss Cross, who lived with the family in Devonshire Street, W. Coincident with the last 'conviction of Mrs. Merrick, another club called John's Club was established on the upper part of the same premises.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHAMPAGNE ON FLOOR.

label: text
text: Some kind of intimation must have been received that a raid was to take place, for the police found the front door barred. It was not until a large hole had been made in the door with a powerful jemmy that the door was opened. That involved a delay of about four or five minutes, and, as was to be expected, there was not much sign of drinking having been taking place, but there was evidence that champagne had been spilt and glasses broken.

label: text
text: The door of the John's Club was also forced by the police and a considerable quantity of liquor was found there. At the time of the raid 119 men and women were present.

label: text
text: Mr. Wilberforce (the magistrate): Do you suggest that this is an attempt to keep the home fires burning?

label: paragraph_title
text: Mr. Muskett: Yes.

label: text
text: Mr. Norman Birkett, K.C., who defended, said that the suggested connection between this and John's Club was denied. When Mrs. Herrick went to prison, she left instructions that her son should keep away from the premises, and he would now give an undertaking never to enter any night club again. Miss Cross was Mrs. Merrick's second cousin. The premises had been run at a loss during Mrs. Merrick's imprisonment.

label: text
text: Merrick and Miss Cross were each fined £75, and Merrick was ordered to pay £52 10s. costs.

label: text
text: The "Star," calling attention to the Australian plans to try out all possible test players, declares: "It is time to protest against the apathy of the Marylebone mandarins, who, after England has suffered a fresh series of disasters, are as supine as ever, and are not devising any schemes to develop young talent. Why cannot England think a year ahead, like Australia does, instead of improving in the face of the foe?"
